questions.question: What operation is allowed in a field but not guaranteed in a general ring?
options: Taking the determinant of every element

questions.question: In a field, which elements must have multiplicative inverses?
What kind of ring is every field?
options: A ring whose addition has no inverses

questions.question: The ring $\mathbb Z_n$ of integers modulo $n$ is a field exactly when:
In a field, if $ab=0$, what must hold?
In the field $\mathbb R$, what is the multiplicative inverse of $5$?
Why is $0$ excluded from the multiplicative inverse condition in a field?
options: Zero is not an element of $\mathbb R$
Zero is not allowed to be added in a field
Zero is always equal to one
No element can multiply by $0$ to give $1$

questions.question: Which structure is a field under the usual operations?
options: The set of all $2\times2$ real matrices with matrix multiplication only

questions.question: A field must contain distinct additive and multiplicative identities $0\ne 1$. Which is the smallest possible field?
Which computation uses the field property of division by a nonzero scalar?
options: Changing a matrix into a set

questions.question: Why is $(\mathbb Z,+,\cdot)$ not a field, despite being a ring with unity?
options: The integers are not closed under multiplication.
Most nonzero integers do not have multiplicative inverses in $\mathbb Z$

questions.question: Why does a field require multiplication to be commutative?
options: It follows from the existence of additive inverses alone
It is false for $\mathbb R$ and $\mathbb C$
It is needed only for finite fields
It is part of the stated field definition

questions.question: What is the relationship between a field and a commutative ring with unity?
options: A field is such a ring with inverses for all nonzero elements
A field drops the distributive laws
A commutative ring with unity is automatically a field.
A field has no additive group structure

questions.question: In which of these sets does $2$ have a multiplicative inverse inside the same set?
Over which of these scalar systems is a usual vector space allowed in the standard definition?
In a field, if $a\ne0$ and $ab=ac$, what follows?
Why is division by zero not rescued by the field axioms?
options: The additive identity must also be the multiplicative identity
The inverse condition explicitly applies only to nonzero elements
Division by zero is allowed only in complex fields

questions.question: Why does the statement “scalars come from a field” matter when solving linear equations?
options: Row scaling and cancellation use scalar inverses
It makes all vector spaces finite-dimensional.
It removes the need for addition

questions.question: In the field $\mathbb C$, what is the inverse of $1+i$?
Suppose scalars are taken from $\mathbb Z$. Which step in Gaussian elimination can fail as a field-based operation?
options: Dividing a row by a nonzero pivot
